description: Aspiring Astronauts that eat Banh Mi
summary:
Banh Mi Munchers Go To Space is a turn-based 2D game made in Unity. Players get to design, launch and fly a lander to either Moon or Mars. They start with a budget and choose a camera, a science instrument, power, a battery, fuel, an antenna, food and a rocket. Every choice adds mass, cost and power demand, and a Launch Check warns them about weak spots before they launch. The mission then lasts a certain amount of days in space and 5 days on the surface. Players spend a few actions each day on downlinks, repairs, course fixes and soil scans while they deal with solar flares, micrometeoroids, battery drain and the cold. Their goals are to map the landing site and find water ice in a permanently shadowed crater.

The game answers the challenge by turning the real trade-offs of mission design into the core gameplay. At the end, a stats screen will grade the mission and explains why it went well or badly. Water ice at the moon's south pole is a key target for NASA’s Artemis program. Our game helps students and the public see why designing a mission takes careful planning, compromise and readiness for risk.
details:
So, what is Banh Mi Munchers Go To Space?

It is a turn-based 2D strategy game. The player gets to run a mission to space. The core concepts are:

  1. Brief: The player learns the goals (map the landing area and the other objective depending on the mission they pick. i.e Moon is finding ice water)
  2. Design the lander: On three tabs (Tools, Resources, Rocket), the player picks a camera, a science instrument, solar panels, a battery, a fuel tank, an antenna, food supplies, and a rocket with boosters. Each part changes mass, cost and power use, all within their allowed budget.
  3. Launching: Depends on how the player design their rocket and lander, launching could fail and potentially lead to an early lost.
  4. Cruise: As the lander detach from the rocket, it slowly travels toward the destination, and this process takes days. Each day the player gets a few action points to spend on things like downlinking data (sends back data for points), repairs (keep the hull up), power saving (save battery), scanning for hazards, etc.
  5. Surface: The player will then land at their destination after the cruising phase. There, they will complete their goals set at the beginning like scanning the soil for ice, takes photos for data. They will also have to maintain their power by tilting the solar panels toward the low polar Sun and manages the battery through freezing nights.
  6. Debrief: The mission gets a score and a grade from S to D, with reasons on what went right, what went wrong, and why.

Benefits

  • Mission design provides a hands-on experience instead of a lecture. Players feel the trade-offs between mass, budget and power for themselves.
  • Every result is explained, so a failed mission still teaches something, and Retry lets the player try again with the same lander.

Intended impact

We want students to understand why NASA missions take years of planning, and why engineers spend so much effort on margins, testing and backup plans. One of the missions is set at the lunar south pole and centered on water ice, so it connects players to the science behind Artemis and future crewed bases on the Moon. We hope it sparks interest in aerospace and STEM careers.

Tools and technologies

  • Engine: Unity 2D
  • Language: C#
  • Art: pixel-art style
  • Design: Canva for the storyboard. Hand-drawn assets imported into Unity
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with research, rule design, the build guide, and code review

Creativity

  • Every part has a real cost. For example, a choice may save money but may increase the mission's risk, and the infrared spectrometer finds ice faster.
  • Space environments force the player to adapt and manage resources accordingly.
  • The results screen turns data into lessons.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific grounding: weak solar power at the south pole, cold nights that drain batteries, and the real role of neutron and infrared instruments in finding water.
  • Fun learning experience: rules are simple but still create meaningful trade-offs.
  • Accessibility: clear wording, tooltips and short play sessions for players of all ages.
  • Scope and time: with about 2 days to build, we optimized a lot of the gameplay and used one fixed landing site, as well as planning Mars as a future mission.
  • Balance: using real data will cause the game is be unbalance so there were changes to numbers, including made-up value to account for balancing.
